edges.description: Merlin restrains the Hippo effectors; losing it releases them. How it does so is contested, and the entry carries that as a discussion rather than choosing: one body of work has merlin recruiting LATS to the plasma membrane, another has it acting in the nucleus on a ubiquitin ligase that inhibits LATS there.
The tumour. The cell type is Schwann, and why this lineage rather than another is the question the cited review says is unanswered.
The tumour as the finding that defines the disease.
A benign tumour in a bony canal. What it does is mechanical, and it is the route to every auditory and vestibular phenotype in this entry.

edges.description: The tumour cells are a source of VEGF, and the tumours carry more and wider vessels than normal nerve. A study in cell lines and mouse models proposes that loss of merlin lowers semaphorin and so tips the balance towards angiogenesis. No cited source tests this route in human tumours, though the 2009 tissue series found semaphorins 3A and 3F in only a fifth of schwannomas (Tumour Angiogenesis). The 2009 authors also say the usual account, VEGF from tumour cells acting on VEGFR-2 on endothelial cells, may be more complex in schwannomas.

The vasculature is taken to sustain the tumour's growth, and so its pressure on the nerve. The cited sources hedge VEGF's part in growth. The clearest human evidence is that blocking VEGF brings a fall in volume of 20% or more at some point in under half of target tumours in the two prospective trials (43%, and 32% during the second's induction; 14% in the first when the fall had to hold), though in six of ten patients in the 2009 series; counting smaller falls, shrinkage is commoner still: nine of ten tumours shrank in the 2009 series, and in the 2016 trial most shrank by 5% or more (the Bevacizumab row).

nodes.description: An anti-VEGF antibody, and the only drug in this entry with a pooled response rate. Across 161 patients and 196 assessable tumours, 41% had partial regression and 47% no change; hearing improved in 20% and was stable in 69%. Seventeen per cent had serious toxicity. A later meta-analysis of 14 cohort studies gave a radiographic response of 30% and a hearing response of 32%. In two prospective trials, a hearing response that held for three months or more came in 36% of patients in the first, with an improvement at any visit, confirmed or not, in 57%, and a hearing response at six months in 41% in the second. A tumour response at some point came in 43% of target tumours in the first trial and in 32% during the second's six-month induction, and in 14% in the first trial when the response had to hold. Neither trial found a significant correlation between hearing and tumour responses. In a post hoc analysis of the second trial, pediatric participants (under 21) had fewer hearing and tumour responses than adults (P = .08 for hearing and P = .05 for tumour response); in a multicentre series of 17 children, most of those with hearing loss improved but only two patients had a radiological response.

nodes.description: The tumours' blood supply. In one series of NF2-related and sporadic schwannomas, every vestibular schwannoma examined expressed VEGF, and NF2-related tumours had more and wider vessels than normal nerve. VEGFR-2 was found on about a third of tumour vessels, which the authors call reduced expression. The tumour cells expressed VEGF and the neuropilins in the pattern of normal nerve, so the tissue data show that VEGF is present, not that it is overexpressed. In the same passage on tumour-cell staining, VEGFR-2 was expressed in about half of the tumours, and semaphorins 3A and 3F in only a fifth, at reduced intensity. What VEGF blockade does to the vessels is measured in mice; in patients it is seen mainly by imaging.

evidence.snippet: A correlation was observed between an increase in tumor volume and hearing loss (r = 0.686; p < 0.001).

evidence.reference_title: Vestibular Schwannoma: What We Know and Where We are Heading.
evidence.snippet: Larger tumours can cause hydrocephalus and brainstem compression leading to symptoms such as facial paraesthesia, vertigo, and headache

nodes.description: The balance disturbance the reviews list among the syndrome's commonest symptoms, attributed by one to the vestibular tumours and by another to larger tumours specifically. The row is bound to vertigo, the specific symptom one of its sources names; the broader phrase balance dysfunction that the other source uses is not what the binding asserts.

nodes.description: Unphosphorylated YAP and TAZ enter the nucleus and drive TEAD-dependent transcription. In a mouse already carrying a Lats1/2 lesion, gene dosage sets how much tumour the animal gets and how long it lives, and one surviving YAP or TAZ allele is enough for a schwannoma to form. That is a statement about how much YAP and TAZ activity the tumour needs, not about a YAP allele initiating one on its own.

biological_processes: TEAD-dependent transcriptional activation by YAP and TAZ

evidence.reference_title: Schwannoma development is mediated by Hippo pathway dysregulation and modified by RAS/MAPK signaling.
evidence.snippet: These data suggest that YAP/TAZ gene dosage determines tumor burden and survival, and that a single allele of YAP or TAZ is sufficient for schwannoma formation.

evidence.reference_title: Merlin/NF2 loss-driven tumorigenesis linked to CRL4(DCAF1)-mediated inhibition of the hippo pathway kinases Lats1 and 2 in the nucleus.
evidence.snippet: There was a strong positive correlation of nuclear YAP staining and weak or absent cytoplasmic P-YAP staining in tumors with low Merlin expression (p=0.001 for YAP and p=0.001 for phospho-YAP, Mann-Whitney U test), indicating that loss of Merlin causes activation of YAP via reduced phosphorylation and increased accumulation in the nucleus.
